title: Finite Galois quasi-splitting of an already semistable curve
statement:
Let $k$ be a field and let $S$ be a normal integral projective finite-type $k$-scheme. Let $f:Q\to S$ be H-projective, flat and finitely presented, with all geometric fibres nonempty connected reduced curves of pure dimension one, and with smooth geometrically integral generic fibre. Suppose every singular point of a geometric fibre has completed local ring $\Omega[[u,v]]/(uv)$ over its algebraically closed residue field $\Omega$. Let a finite group $H$ act on $k,Q,S$ compatibly with $f$. There are a finite group $J$, a surjection $\rho:J\to H$, a normal integral projective finite-type $k$-scheme $S'$, an equivariant finite surjective generically etale morphism $b:S'\to S$, and a compatible $J$-action on $Q'=Q\times_S S'$. Writing $N=\ker\rho$, one has $k(S')^N=k(S)$. Every fibre of $Q'\to S'$ is quasi-split: its singular points and both points above each singular point in the normalization are rational over the residue field of the base point. A point is rational when its residue-field map from that field is an isomorphism. This includes smooth fibres, with empty sets of singular points. More generally, for any quasi-split nodal family, quasi-splitting is preserved by arbitrary base change of its base: over each new residue field all singular points and both normalization branches above them remain rational.

Field, integral scheme, proper morphism, finite type, geometric integrality, projectivity, finite morphism, surjectivity, function field and field extensions use [def-weil-field], [def-pc-integral-scheme], [def-weil-proper-morphism], [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], [def-pc-geometrically-irreducible], [def-kun-projective], [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], [def-weil-surjective-morphism], [def-sc-function-field], [def-pc-field-extension] and [def-pc-field-tower]. H-projective means admitting a closed immersion into a finite-dimensional projective space over the target; it does not refer to a group named H. A normal scheme has integrally closed domains as local rings. An alteration is a proper surjective morphism of integral schemes, finite over a dense open of the target. A purely inseparable extension in characteristic p>0 means that every element has some p-power in the smaller field; in characteristic zero it means equality. All group actions below are by scheme or field automorphisms, and are allowed to be nonfaithful.

Flatness, finite presentation, smoothness, geometric fibres, closed immersions, fibre products and dimension use [def-weil-flat-morphism], [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation], [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], [def-weil-geometric-fibre], [def-weil-closed-immersion], [def-pc-fibre-product] and [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. Etale uses [def-weil-etale-morphism].

Normalization, maximal-ideal-adic completion and formal power series use [def-weil-pbc-reduced-normalization], [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion] and [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series].

proof.text: For a flat finitely presented nodal family $g:C\to V$, use the branch-scheme criterion. For an arbitrary base change $V'\to V$ and $v'\mapsto v$, write $F=\kappa(v)$, $E=\kappa(v')$. The branch-cover base-change identification gives $(B_{g_{V'}})_{v'}=(B_g)_v\times_F E$. For a quasi-split fibre this is a disjoint union of $\operatorname{Spec}E$, since $F\otimes_F E=E$; the criterion makes every node and both branches $E$-rational. Thus quasi-splitting is preserved by arbitrary base change, without a Noetherian hypothesis on $V'$.

source.place: Definition before Lemma 5.7, pp.614--615; preservation used in Theorem 5.9, p.617.

proof.text: Each intermediate normal integral projective finite-type $k$-base $V$ is Noetherian and finite dimensional, by finite type over the Noetherian field $k$ and the dimension lemma. With empty marking, the pulled-back family remains flat finitely presented and nodal by semistable base change. Projectivity survives base change and implies properness, so its branch scheme is finite. Induct simultaneously over every such base $V$, its finite group $G$, and every projective flat finitely presented nodal family $C\to V$ with reduced pure one-dimensional geometric fibres and compatible $G$-actions on $k,V,C$, without generic smoothness. The claim is the finite equivariant quasi-splitting cover with surjective group map and exact kernel fixed field. Use strong induction on the bad closure dimension, with empty closure the identity case.

source.place: Lemma 5.7 hypotheses and finite-dimensional induction, p.615.

proof.text: For the current family $g:C\to V$, put $A=\{v:C_v\text{ is not quasi-split}\}$ and $Z=\overline A$. Generic spreading is supplied by the branch-spreading lemma. The bad-locus lemma puts the finitely many component generic points $s_i$ of $Z$ in $A$. If $Z$ is empty, take the identity cover and group map. Otherwise set $E_i=(B_g)_{s_i}$, finite etale by the branch-cover lemma.

source.place: Lemma 5.7 first paragraph and beginning of second paragraph, p.615.

proof.text: Apply equivariant finite residue domination to $V$, its current group $G$, the $s_i$ and $E_i$. It gives $a:W\to V$, $\sigma:J\twoheadrightarrow G$, a normal integral projective finite-type base, a finite surjective generically etale cover, and $k(W)^{\ker\sigma}=k(V)$. Every branch fibre above every $s_i$ splits, so every such curve fibre is quasi-split by the criterion and branch base change. Give $C\times_V W$ the action $j(c,w)=(\sigma(j)c,jw)$; both projections are equivariant because their coordinates have the same image in $V$.

On $W$, Step 1 gives $A_W\subseteq a^{-1}(A)$, and Step 2 with branch spreading verifies the spreading hypothesis on every integral reduced closed subscheme of $W$. Step 4 splits all points over the $s_i$, so the bad-locus lemma makes $Z_W=\overline{A_W}$ empty or of smaller dimension. Apply induction on $W$ and compose the resulting cover with $a$. The cover-composition lemma gives finiteness, surjectivity, generic etaleness and the exact composite-kernel fixed field. Start at $(V,G,C)=(S,H,Q)$; fibre-product associativity identifies the final family with $Q\times_S S'$. Induction gives its quasi-split fibres; Step 1 supplies the independent base-change clause.
